items.content:
RT @Kostastsale: I found an exposed directory through Hunt io containing a Russian-language CLAUDE.md that looks like an operational playbook for AI-assisted exploitation.

The workflow:

Find leaked credentials -> enumerate the target stack -> test LFI/RCE/SQLi/IDOR/business logic -> avoid rate limits -> establish access -> move on.

It specifically tells the operator not to waste time brute-forcing passwords before finding something critical.

Alongside it are scripts for SharePoint key extraction, TeamCity, SonicWall SMA 1000, BeyondTrust, SmarterMail and LoadMaster. .bash_history also shows repeated OpenCode use across multiple targets.

Do we think this is a pentest or a real threat actor? 😂 I think the latter lol

Pay attention to how closely this matches the boring reality of a lot of intrusion activity...

Known vulns. Exposed management interfaces. Leaked credentials. Secrets. Weak auth. Misconfigurations. Automation to enumerate and exploit faster.

That is what defenders should be hunting continuously.

We spend a lot of time talking about advanced sandbox evasion, novel malware and APT tradecraft because it makes better headlines. Meanwhile, a huge amount of real-world access still starts with very basic stuff that someone bothered to look for.

AI just makes that workflow faster and easier to scale.

Also, ssh-authorized_keys and files named ssh-jagarzon are in the screenshot.

APT Jagarzon confirmed? 😂 Absolutely not lol

RT @chrisrohlf: This response of “that’s not how security works, it’s about balancing tradeoffs with the business” is not unfamiliar to me. I empathize, but that mindset is precisely why the security industry, and many ‘Information Security’ programs at big companies, find themselves struggling to meet the task of securing themselves with or from agents in this new era.

Risk tracking spreadsheets, the phishing education, the threat intel, the manual appsec etc. None of these things were built for the challenges we are facing now. What got us here won’t get us there. We need to be willing to make big changes to how we do things if we want to solve or even keep pace with these problems.

RT @IntCyberDigest: ❗️ An AI agent broke out of its virtual machine and triggered a use-after-free in Google's heavily hardened hypervisor by tricking KVM into quietly rewriting a memory-mapping entry with a single three-byte instruction.

It then flooded the host with 49,152 memory mappings until KVM followed a pointer into that freed memory, and on its fourth live attempt the host handed over Google's secret flag.

No one gave it an exploit, so the agent spent weeks studying KVM's source code and wrote 14,338 lines of harness code to get there.

RT @rickcsong: The internet needs proof of humanness more than ever. We have a unique opportunity to build it with privacy at the core.

As bots become harder to stop and identity theft grows more sophisticated, platforms increasingly need stronger ways to verify who’s real. But stronger verification shouldn’t have to mean collecting more personal data.

We should be asking not just what data is needed, but also what data isn’t.

That’s what the team at @withpersona is working toward with Relay.

Relay uses Privacy Pass, an open IETF standard, to let organizations verify claims like humanness or age without learning your identity, all while preserving the best-in-class accuracy of Persona’s platform.

Proud of the team for the work on this one. Excited to see where it goes

items.content:
RT @DavidSacks: Nvidia’s OpenShell announcement is a reminder that agent safety is an engineering problem.

Recent breakouts weren’t proof that development must stop. They were proof that the sandbox was too weak. The runtime environment was poorly designed and misconfigured.

The right response is open runtime isolation, control of the path to the model, out-of-band hardware enforcement, and a faster pace of safety work with the frontier labs.

As the technical blog puts it: “We believe we need to increase the pace of AI safety research and engineering in collaboration with frontier labs and the broader community.”

That’s how you earn trust. Not by virtue-signaling a pause, and not by acting like no solution exists.

A security team messaged me today to say thanks... They ran one of their domains through it this morning, and found an issue they didn't know was there. Honestly that made my day!! 🥳

It started as a small tool I built for myself, and now it does what I always wanted: you put in a domain and in about 30 seconds you see what's wrong with its DNS. Dangling records, lame delegation, no DNSSEC, weak SPF/DMARC, missing registrar locks, old subdomains nobody remembers creating

You don't need to install anything or give it access to your zones... it just looks at your domain from the outside, like anyone on the internet can.

The screenshot is from a real scan. A nameserver that stopped answering but is still in the delegation. Nobody notices these until someone else does.

Try it on your own domain, and tell me what it finds: https://t.co/7i64HAHVEB
items.author: NetAskari

items.content:
it’s not impossible, but it’s also not easy. it requires a lot of work.

existing tech like firecracker has held up very well against current models, including gpt-6/mythos level models. completely blocking egress is relatively straightforward. things get much harder when the task requires constrained internet access, which is what led to most openai sanboc bypasses, but even then, it’s possible.

BUT, the mistake would be assuming firecracker will also hold against something like gpt-7 or gpt-8, its literally the kind of assumption is how you end up with much more catastrophic hugging face style incidents.

you need to assume firecracker can eventually be broken and build the surrounding system around that assumption. also, you need to assume a lot of controls we thought would hold will fail and build around it. and, lots of sandbox escape auditing with models and humans before you do large scale training or evals.

it is never easy, if security or developer could anticipate every vulnerability beforehand and design things, security would be a solved problem, and there is a reason its not

items.content:
RT @vxunderground: AI is cool and badass. I like it.

No, it's not the end of the world. We can "contain" it.

Now I will rant for a moment about what I dislike about AI.

I strongly dislike when large corporations try to inject AI into every product, essentially forcing us to use AI.

I also strongly dislike when people use AI for every small little thing in their life, such as leaving comments on websites like Xitter, YouTube, Reddit, etc. It defeats the entire purpose of leaving a comment on something... you're supposed to share YOUR thoughts, not an AI agents generated string output. It's goofy.

I also strongly dislike the nonsense blabbering of AI propaganda, how it will destroy the world, or how companies need to "contain it", essentially acting as means to corner the AI model market, trying to strip it away from individuals who may want to host it locally. It's a facade of "Only WE can do AI, not YOU", whilst charging absurd fees for usage.

I also dislike AI nerds who try to tell me to use AI to do things I do simply because I enjoy doing them. Yes, maybe an AI agent could reverse engineer faster than me, or code faster than me, but I do it because I enjoy it.

AI is an excellent tool to enhance work flows, or learn (assuming it doesn't hallucinate).

Okay, that's all I want to say about AI for today.

RT @LeakerApple: Apple is using several specifications of Samsung and LG panels in the iPhone 18 Pro this year.

Samsung G9N, G9P, G9Q.
LG GVC, GH3.

Not only does there seem to be panel variations between suppliers, but also between panel specifications. There will always be slight variance between panels, but I don’t remember this ever being a big issue since they‘re all built to Apple’s spec and calibrated. 

This situation might also explain why Apple managed to negotiate lower prices for displays this year, because they’re using more LG panels.

items.content:
RT @vxunderground: AI is cool and badass. I like it.

No, it's not the end of the world. We can "contain" it.

Now I will rant for a moment about what I dislike about AI.

I strongly dislike when large corporations try to inject AI into every product, essentially forcing us to use AI.

I also strongly dislike when people use AI for every small little thing in their life, such as leaving comments on websites like Xitter, YouTube, Reddit, etc. It defeats the entire purpose of leaving a comment on something... you're supposed to share YOUR thoughts, not an AI agents generated string output. It's goofy.

I also strongly dislike the nonsense blabbering of AI propaganda, how it will destroy the world, or how companies need to "contain it", essentially acting as means to corner the AI model market, trying to strip it away from individuals who may want to host it locally. It's a facade of "Only WE can do AI, not YOU", whilst charging absurd fees for usage.

I also dislike AI nerds who try to tell me to use AI to do things I do simply because I enjoy doing them. Yes, maybe an AI agent could reverse engineer faster than me, or code faster than me, but I do it because I enjoy it.

AI is an excellent tool to enhance work flows, or learn (assuming it doesn't hallucinate).

Okay, that's all I want to say about AI for today.
